steps.title: Stack: last in, first out
steps.content: A stack (LIFO) removes the most recently added item first. The main operations are push (add), pop (remove top) and peek (read top).
steps.example: Push A, then B, then C. The next pop returns C.

steps.title: Trace a stack
steps.prompt: Push 2, then 5, then 7. What is returned by the next pop?
steps.explanation: 7 was pushed last, so LIFO returns 7 first.

steps.title: Queue: first in, first out
steps.content: A queue (FIFO) removes the earliest added item first. Enqueue adds at the rear; dequeue removes from the front.
steps.example: Enqueue A, B, C. The next dequeue returns A.

steps.title: Choose a queue use
steps.prompt: Which situation most naturally uses a FIFO queue?
steps.explanation: A printer queue normally handles jobs in the order they arrive.

steps.title: Where they appear
steps.content: Stacks help with function calls, undo operations, expression evaluation and balanced brackets. Queues help with scheduling, breadth-first search and request processing.
steps.tip: When a problem says 'most recent first', think stack. When it says 'arrival order', think queue.

questions.prompt: Which principle does a stack follow?
questions.explanation: A stack is last in, first out.

questions.prompt: Which operation removes the top item from a stack?
questions.explanation: Pop removes and returns the top item.

questions.prompt: Which principle does a queue follow?
questions.explanation: A queue is first in, first out.

questions.prompt: Which data structure is commonly used for breadth-first search?
questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue to process nodes in discovery order.

questions.prompt: A stack receives 4, 6, 8. Two pops return:
questions.explanation: The top is 8; after popping it, 6 becomes the top.
